Reading a contract, matching it against the schedule, and saying plainly what it will cost us is a task these systems are already good at, it needs no frontier model to do, and doing it well confers no advantage over anybody else — the value is in not being cheated, which everyone can have at once.
So the technology cuts both ways against the same institutions.
Pointed at a capped world it is an equalizer, handing everyone the verification that used to require a lawyer.
Pointed at an uncapped one it is a solvent, dissolving the caps by being fluent, and turning the same fluency into an advantage for whoever has the most of it.
In a contest the knee never rescues us, however steeply absolute returns diminish, because payoff rides on *relative* performance and the marginal value of compute is set by the prize and the opponent rather than by the production function: sampling error shrinks with the square root of the budget on both sides, and the pick-off still goes to whoever holds the tighter error bars.
@Shahidi2025Coasean have both branches on one page, as opposing forces on the price of an agent: returns to agent quality that diminish until agents commoditize like search, and prices that rise with the stakes of a transaction because quality depends on compute.
Those are not two forces on one price but the two regimes, and which one a transaction lands in is decided by whether the rulebook has already made it a decision problem.
So the class of negotiations where the cheapest subsidy is also the most effective one is exactly the class the rulebook has already converted from contest to decision.

## Point the agents at the rulebook

Where does that leave the disagreement?
Not at “agents won’t help.”
The plainest statement I can manage: the efficiency on offer from cheap negotiation-compute is small beside the efficiency already embodied in the boring institutional technology — standard forms, damage schedules, chartered associations, all of it settled and amortized — and so the live margin is in improving that technology, now perhaps with machine help, rather than in bypassing it.

Which suggests where to look, and what to distrust while looking.
The small cases will work.
Roommates dividing chores, an office arguing about the thermostat, a strata committee and its parking: these are the cases where I expect agent negotiators to be a plain delight, and I do not think the enthusiasm is misplaced.
But it is worth being clear about *why* they work, because the reason is not that bargaining scales.
They work because they arrive with the caps pre-installed: few enough things at stake that $m$ is small, few enough people that the bargain is bounded, and a custom or a convention already standing in for a pinned division.
The rules we had to impose by fiat are, in a household, simply the furniture.

That sets a trap I would rather name in advance.
Every pilot will look like evidence for the general programme, and none of it will be, because the thing doing the work in a successful pilot is invisible exactly when it is working.
A demonstration that agents can settle a parking dispute tells us nothing about a catchment, in the same way that a demonstration of a bridge over a creek tells us nothing about a span across a strait, and for the same reason: it is the size that was carrying the design.

And a demonstration failing upward is not the worst case.
Removing the caps at scale does not return us to the status quo — it starts a game whose returns to compute the well-resourced side is best placed to collect, which is extraction, and whose contest costs come out of the surplus, which is dissipation.
The downside is not that the utopia fails to arrive; it is a worse division than the clumsy rules were already producing, arrived at faster and with better documentation.

So if I had to put the constructive reading in one line: point the agents at the rulebook rather than at each other.
The caps are the design surface — where to draw a boundary, how long a menu to allow, what formula tracks harm closely enough to keep the deals that should close from failing.

<!-- phase two: cake-cutting to a footnote. -->

I want to be careful about how much that promises, because the obvious optimistic case for it is wrong.
Designing the rules is not a soft problem that yields to a machine that is good at hard ones.
Automated mechanism design is itself NP-hard [@Conitzer2002Complexity], and it has an unpleasant shape: searching over rules means evaluating each candidate, and evaluating a candidate means solving the game it induces, which is the exponential thing we were running from, now in the inner loop.
Fair division is the cautionary tale rather than the promise.
Envy-free cake cutting for an arbitrary number of players was a famous open problem, and when @Aziz2016Discretea settled it the protocol they produced needs, in the worst case, $a^{a^{a^{a^{a^a}}}}$ queries^[Queries in the Robertson–Webb model: each one is either a cut, or an evaluation of a piece.] — writing $a$ for the players, since our $n$ is spoken for.
Three players have had a workable protocol since Selfridge and Conway found one independently, around 1960 and 1993, neither of them ever publishing it [@Procaccia2013Cake]; Aziz and Mackenzie in a companion paper gave four players a protocol finishing inside 203 queries [@Aziz2016Discrete].
From five players upward the only bounded procedure known is that tower, and truncating it to its top three levels already names a number with more than $10^{2000}$ digits.
Nothing about being good at proofs makes that number smaller.

Three things nonetheless make the rulebook the better place to spend the cognition, and only the third is a matter of principle.
Design is amortized: a rule devised once governs bargains for decades, so the question is never whether the search was cheap but whether it was cheap per use, which is the same arithmetic that made institutions worth settling in the first place.
Design is low-dimensional: we are not searching the space of all conceivable mechanisms, we are choosing $\bar n$, choosing $\bar m$, and picking a formula out of a small family, with each candidate testable by simulation against sampled populations rather than by worst-case analysis.
And design tolerates approximation, which bargaining does not.
This is the Shalizi asymmetry^[Shalizi’s argument against central planning [@Shalizi2012Soviet] is that the planner’s problem is one enormous optimization, and that one solve of the Soviet plan would take a modern solver about a thousand years. In his accounting the plan need only come within a tolerance $\epsilon$ of the optimum, and loosening $\epsilon$ saves almost no time, but the planner is at least licensed to round the answer and declare the plan close enough, where a bargaining system has nobody entitled to say that.] read forwards: the planner’s epsilon is a tolerance, and rule-making is a planner-like act, so a rulebook that captures ninety per cent of the available surplus is a good rulebook — where a *bargain* that leaves ten per cent on the table has funded the coalition that comes to break it.
Approximation is safe on the design side of the line and self-undermining on the bargaining side, which is a reason to move the compute across that line regardless of whether design is cheap.

What none of this touches is the half that was never computational.
Where $\bar n$ falls decides who is inside the bargain and who is merely downstream of it; the formula decides who gets shortchanged when it cannot track harms it is not permitted to ask about; and those are contested, by the same parties, with nobody outside to enforce the contest’s own rules — the political Coase theorem [@Acemoglu2003Why] that this whole essay has been deferring since we first turned $k$.
A very good optimizer hands us a frontier of rulebooks and no way to choose among them.
So: not a retreat from Krier’s ambition, and not a promise that the machines will do our constitutional thinking for us.
The same ambition, aimed one level up, at the layer where a good answer compounds — and where the remaining difficulty is one we will have to argue about rather than compute.
Regulation sits where it sits because that is where bargaining failed the first time we ran the experiment, at speech speed, over centuries; the regulatory state reads to me less like an imposition on the market than like a map of the market’s historical no-go terrain.
Cheap cognition will redraw that map.
The claim this post stakes is that it redraws it from inside the institutions, not from above them.
